The report does not confirm an Apple product or its features; it argues that Apple should consider lessons from Lenovo’s convertible laptop.

The distinction matters. Touch on a laptop can mean more than tapping icons on a display. In the Yoga 9n, the stylus can be used for note-taking, drawing and photo retouching, while the trackpad offers another surface for pen input without placing a hand over the screen.

The Verge describes the Yoga 9n as a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with an OLED display and a stylus included. Its hinge folds back into tent and tablet modes, while the device can also work as a conventional clamshell laptop. In tablet mode, it can be held in landscape or portrait orientation.

Those positions change how the laptop fits into everyday use. The report says folding the keyboard out of the way is useful for watching movies, playing games with a controller or adding the laptop to a multi-monitor desk setup with a separate keyboard and mouse. The same machine can shift between those roles without being limited to a single screen-and-keyboard arrangement.

The pen experience is the feature the reviewer wants Apple to study. The Yoga’s stylus works directly on the display, but also on its haptic trackpad, which the report compares to a Wacom-like experience. That option lets someone draw or retouch without covering the part of the screen they need to see.

The reviewer says the stylus is especially convenient for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. It is a return to pen-based work after giving up an older Wacom device, the report says, and having the choice of screen or trackpad makes the pen useful in more situations.

The Yoga’s stylus attaches magnetically to the laptop lid, either by itself or while in its case. Lenovo’s pen charges through USB-C. The Verge reviewer says a future Apple Pencil for a touchscreen MacBook should attach to the laptop and support wireless charging, so it stays charged and ready to use.

That is a practical difference for owners. A pen that has a dedicated place on the laptop is less likely to be left elsewhere, while charging it as it attaches would avoid treating the stylus as another accessory that needs separate attention. Those are hopes expressed by the reviewer, not confirmed details about Apple hardware.

The report also questions whether Apple would simply make a conventional convertible. The reviewer argues that swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED display for a touchscreen OLED panel, or copying the familiar 2-in-1 design, would not feel like a distinctive Apple approach. One alternative raised is a design similar to the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio, which brings the touchscreen forward instead of folding it backward. The writer also leaves room for a different design altogether.

Software could shape whether touch feels natural or awkward. The Verge points to hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating Golden Gate to make touch functions feel less like poking at controls built for a mouse cursor. The report says using desktop operating systems with a finger or stylus can feel clunky, even on enjoyable Windows laptops and Chromebooks.

Apple has not confirmed the rumored MacBook or its price. The Verge reviewer expects a touchscreen MacBook Pro to be expensive and says Apple’s recent design choices have not all worked well, citing the HomeView’s lack of apps, the iPhone Duo and the earlier butterfly keyboard problems. The report’s central request is specific: let a stylus work on the trackpad as well as the display.

The Mac vs. PC debate has been going on for years . I maintain there’s no “right” answer — it all depends on what you’re looking for. But let’s get a little more specific: Which is a better main driver, the ThinkPad or the MacBook? Both laptop lines are powerful, versatile, and available in several configurations, and both are among the most widely used laptops for work, school, and everyday tasks. Each has carved out a niche for itself based on its strengths. Also: Apple’s $599 MacBook Neo hands-on: The budget laptop we’ve all been waiting for? Apple’s MacBook lineup aims to handle creative tasks flawlessly, offers a rich ecosystem of integration, but may struggle with gaming performance and compatibility. Lenovo ThinkPads have lots of ports, great keyboards, and are durable enough to be used in space , but require navigation through an extensive catalog to find the right model. Both are well-equipped to deal with demanding workloads, and both run the gamut in price. Let’s take a closer look at these two product lines. ThinkPads’ distinct boxy black-and-red design has remained largely unchanged since the lineup’s creation in 1992. It’s not exactly “pretty” or flashy, but that’s not a bad thing; you know what they say about trying to fix what isn’t broken. In fact, this continuity of design is part of the whole appeal. The ThinkPad is a no-nonsense, reliable workhorse that doesn’t employ gimmicky designs or fad features. Instead, it uses one standard physical form and diversifies the hardware for different price points and use cases. The ThinkPad’s keyboard, for example, is widely regarded as being exceptionally functional, as are the physical left and right buttons above the trackpad, the red TrackPoint for precision pointing, and extensive port options. Instead of experimental LED lighting and zero-lattice keyboards , the ThinkPad sticks to what works. Also: I tried Lenovo’s modular ThinkBook laptop, and it’s a concept I’d actually root for That isn’t to say it doesn’t have gorgeous displays or isn’t premium. Take the ThinkPad P1 Gen 8 , for example, which has a brilliant 16-inch tandem OLED screen, haptic trackpad, and impressive suite of high-end hardware. If you want a brilliant display or a sleeker form factor, certain models have them — you just have to navigate the catalog. Simply put: There is a ThinkPad for every use case (and budget). The extensive lineup consists of the entry-level E series, the mid-range L series, the premium T and X series, and the top-of-the-line X1 and P series. At the low end, you can find models for a few hundred dollars. Conversely, top-tier mobile workstations in the P series can approach $5,000. Also: A month with Lenovo’s most powerful ThinkPad changed my mind about work laptops Within each of these lines, there are several models and hardware configurations, with lots of customizations available at the point of sale. This flexibility applies to the laptops themselves, which come with extensive ports and are well-suited for outfitting large teams that need backwards compatibility. And of course, with discrete GPUs and lots of RAM, ThinkPads are well-equipped to handle a range of use cases, from everyday productivity tasks to demanding graphical workflows to gaming. ThinkPads can also come preloaded with Windows or Linux and feature far more software flexibility than MacBooks, which are locked to MacOS. Components of a ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 Aura Edition Apple’s MacBooks are infamous for being difficult to repair. It has proprietary components, requires specialized tools, and some models feature soldered RAM and batteries. This is by design: Apple has monetized its repair business by keeping its users within its ecosystem and gatekeeping the process. By contrast, ThinkPads are generally easier for the end user to upgrade and repair, and Lenovo is doubling down on this distinction with recent upgrades. At CES 2026, it unveiled the ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 Aura Edition with a redesigned double-sided motherboard dubbed the “Space Frame”. This allows for easier access to key components, earning a repairability score of 9 out of 10 from iFixit . Also: Buying your next Windows laptop? This Lenovo with a tandem OLED display is my top pick Then, at MWC 2026 in Barcelona, Lenovo showed off its ThinkBook Modular AI PC proof of concept, featuring plug-and-play swappable ports and a detachable keyboard and second display. These modular concepts show a willingness to include swappable, repairable elements in its laptops in a way that Apple has never come close to. If you have an iPhone, your MacBook is a natural extension of your phone in multiple ways. You can answer and respond to messages, take FaceTime video calls, transfer photos or files with one tap, and mirror your iPhone with the Phone app — allowing you to make calls directly with your laptop. Also: The new MacBook Pro gives you M5 Pro and Max power now – for a bigger price All of this is seamless and native — there’s no special apps you have to download, and no software compatibility issues to worry about. Apple has, by far, the most seamless cross-device functionality, and if you have an iPhone, Apple Watch, iPad, or AirPods, they all “just work” out of the box. Windows PCs like ThinkPads don’t come anywhere close to this kind of synergy. Also: The new MacBook Air M5 costs $100 more – here’s what that gets you But you don’t need the latest high-end MacBook Pro model. The thin and light MacBook Air M4 from 2025 is a fantastic laptop for creatives with a gorgeous Liquid Retina display, standard 16GB of unified RAM, and support for two external monitors — all with 18 hours of battery life. MacBooks come ready to go out of the box with capable video editing software and the hardware to back it up, and they’re equally suited to both pro and everyday creators. By contrast, although there are certainly ThinkPad models suitable for creative tasks, like the ThinkPad P1 (Gen 8) , the number of models is more limited. Let’s face it: MacBooks have some of the best build quality out there, with brilliant Liquid Retina XDR displays, high-quality builds, haptic trackpads, and ultraportable form factors. The durable, aluminum unibody laptop chassis is sleek, distinctive, and reflects an overarching design philosophy. Even the M1 MacBook Pro from five years ago (a laptop I used for several months last year) has a more brilliant display than some of the low-end ThinkPads from this year, which look clunky in comparison. Also: 3 Apple devices you shouldn’t buy this month, and 10 I recommend This applies to all MacBooks — from the 13-inch MacBook Air to the most premium MacBook Pro Max. You don’t have to sort through a catalog of several different series to find the one model with the sleek build; Apple has achieved a strong, unified design across its products, and, in turn, raised the bar for the competition. I hate to hedge here, but I really am a fan of both; it just depends on what you’re looking for. For everyday tasks and creative workflows, it’s MacBook all the way. MacOS is stable and efficient, and since I have an iPhone, the integration is unbeatable. I’d happily use a MacBook as my main driver for personal use, especially for commuting. When it comes to a work laptop (for non-creative workflows), it’s hard to beat the ThinkPad’s overall compatibility and flexibility. Plus, when it comes to gaming — although ThinkPads aren’t known to be gaming-first devices — certain models offer solid gaming performance and far more options than a Mac, especially the higher-end X1 or P series models with discrete graphics cards. extraction.body: It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook. Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs. The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse. [Image: 2-in-1s can be seen as a weird compromise between laptops and tablets. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky. My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

extraction.body: The Verge’s hands-on experience with Lenovo’s Yoga 9n points to features that could make a touchscreen MacBook more useful: a stylus that works on both the… The Verge says a touchscreen MacBook may be announced next week, and its experience with Lenovo’s Yoga 9n offers a concrete idea of what could make Apple’s laptop more useful: a stylus that works on both the screen and the trackpad. The report does not confirm an Apple product or its features; it argues that Apple should consider lessons from Lenovo’s convertible laptop. The distinction matters. Touch on a laptop can mean more than tapping icons on a display. In the Yoga 9n, the stylus can be used for note-taking, drawing and photo retouching, while the trackpad offers another surface for pen input without placing a hand over the screen. The Verge describes the Yoga 9n as a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with an OLED display and a stylus included. Its hinge folds back into tent and tablet modes, while the device can also work as a conventional clamshell laptop. In tablet mode, it can be held in landscape or portrait orientation. Those positions change how the laptop fits into everyday use. The report says folding the keyboard out of the way is useful for watching movies, playing games with a controller or adding the laptop to a multi-monitor desk setup with a separate keyboard and mouse. The same machine can shift between those roles without being limited to a single screen-and-keyboard arrangement. The pen experience is the feature the reviewer wants Apple to study. The Yoga’s stylus works directly on the display, but also on its haptic trackpad, which the report compares to a Wacom-like experience. That option lets someone draw or retouch without covering the part of the screen they need to see. The reviewer says the stylus is especially convenient for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. It is a return to pen-based work after giving up an older Wacom device, the report says, and having the choice of screen or trackpad makes the pen useful in more situations. The Yoga’s stylus attaches magnetically to the laptop lid, either by itself or while in its case. Lenovo’s pen charges through USB-C. The Verge reviewer says a future Apple Pencil for a touchscreen MacBook should attach to the laptop and support wireless charging, so it stays charged and ready to use. That is a practical difference for owners. A pen that has a dedicated place on the laptop is less likely to be left elsewhere, while charging it as it attaches would avoid treating the stylus as another accessory that needs separate attention. Those are hopes expressed by the reviewer, not confirmed details about Apple hardware. The report also questions whether Apple would simply make a conventional convertible. The reviewer argues that swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED display for a touchscreen OLED panel, or copying the familiar 2-in-1 design, would not feel like a distinctive Apple approach. One alternative raised is a design similar to the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio, which brings the touchscreen forward instead of folding it backward. The writer also leaves room for a different design altogether. Software could shape whether touch feels natural or awkward. The Verge points to hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating Golden Gate to make touch functions feel less like poking at controls built for a mouse cursor. The report says using desktop operating systems with a finger or stylus can feel clunky, even on enjoyable Windows laptops and Chromebooks. Apple has not confirmed the rumored MacBook or its price. The Verge reviewer expects a touchscreen MacBook Pro to be expensive and says Apple’s recent design choices have not all worked well, citing the HomeView’s lack of apps, the iPhone Duo and the earlier butterfly keyboard problems. The report’s central request is specific: let a stylus work on the trackpad as well as the display. The English-language global edition of JournalArta.

sources.title: BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF Lost $165 Million in a Week. Is Wall Street Pulling Back? - Yahoo Finance
passages: The current flow data does not strongly indicate that Wall Street is retreating from Bitcoin.
A $228.4 million outflow against a backdrop of $104.3 billion in assets appears more like investors taking profits after a significant 25.4% price increase rather than a long-term pullback.
Furthermore, BlackRock's iShares platform recorded $135 billion in net inflows in the third quarter, and institutions looking to reduce risk would likely show up in these numbers first.
These ETFs hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, so a net outflow means investors withdrew more money than they invested.
IBIT drove 72% of $228 million in Bitcoin ETF outflows, yet that figure equals just 0.2% of the $104 billion held in these funds.

Other funds also posted losses, including the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( CBOE: FBTC ), which lost $60.2 million; the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ( NYSEARCA: BTC ), which fell $7.6 million; and the Invesco Galaxy Bitcoin ETF, which lost $4.1 million.
The trend continued into the week's final session, when U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $82.4 million on October 16, with IBIT accounting for $71.8 million of that total.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
A single October 14 selling session generated $261 million in outflows, exceeding the entire week's net withdrawal on its own.
BlackRock's recent performance also tells a positive story.
A 1.7% drop over the week feels relatively mild given the substantial outflows, although on a longer timeline, Bitcoin is down 6.8% this year and 23.4% in the past year.

Investors have pulled about $1.1 billion from U.S. spot Ether ( CRYPTO: ETH ) ETFs over the last three weeks, and the selling hasn’t stopped . These funds directly hold ETH, so when investors withdraw, they often have to sell coins to meet demand. This situation has also significantly impacted Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ), which serves as the custodian for most U.S. spot crypto ETFs. On October 23, 2026, Coinbase shares closed at about $164, down 17% over the past month. So what could attract ETF buyers back into the market? Ethereum spot ETFs have steadily lost funds, with net outflows of $542.1 million recorded from October 5 to 9, according to SoSoValue. Another $320 million followed in outflows from October 12 to 16. The trend persisted with an additional $225 million leaving over just four trading days from October 19 to 22, including a striking $110.5 million on October 22 alone. The complete figures for October 23 are still pending. Notably, one fund drove most of the withdrawals. BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ: ETHA ) saw approximately $1.01 billion exit during this timeframe, accounting for about 93% of the total outflows. Its net assets fell from roughly $9.9 billion on October 5 to around $7.8 billion on October 23—the day it recorded zero flows. Between October 19 and October 22, ETHA’s withdrawals totaled about $233 million, surpassing the $225 million total outflow for all funds in the same period. This suggests that while money is moving out of ETHA, some investors are reallocating their funds to other Ether ETFs, keeping their investment within the Ethereum ecosystem. Yield competition is the first factor. Many investors are attracted to staking options , which involve locking up ETH to help secure the Ethereum network in exchange for rewards. Staking funds distribute this yield to their shareholders. BlackRock also manages the iShares Staked Ethereum Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: ETHB ), meaning traditional Ether funds now compete with income-focused options. Falling prices are the second. ETH has dropped 11.5% in October, trading around $2,361 and is down 20% year-to-date. Falling prices can trigger ETF redemptions, creating a cycle of further selling pressure. Development delays are the third. On October 22, Ethereum developers announced a delay in the Glamsterdam upgrade’s test on the Hoodi network, initially scheduled for October 26. The Ethereum Foundation said developers need more time to assess how a proposed change interacts with existing smart contracts. Without a new timeline, this is another setback for ETH holders seeking immediate catalysts. Despite these outflows, the funds still hold $14.6 billion in net assets, compared to $12.7 billion in total net inflows. This discrepancy exists because ETH prices have risen since most of that investment was made, meaning early holders may still see profits despite recent downturns. Coinbase benefits from custody and ETH staking, so a decline in ETH demand affects its revenue streams. In its Q2 2026 earnings report released on July 30, Coinbase reported an 18.5% year-over-year revenue drop to $1.22 billion. Platform assets also fell from $294 billion to $246 billion, with executives citing ETF outflows as a contributing factor. In discussions with analysts, Coinbase’s Alesia Haas stated, “When customers store with us, they transact with us.” This works both ways—fewer stored assets reduce trading revenue. Over the past week, Coinbase’s stock slipped 5%, while it’s down 27.3% year-to-date. Large transactions have also drawn attention. Whale Alert reported transfers such as 38,236 ETH, valued at $91.7 million, moving into Coinbase Institutional and another 37,568 ETH, worth $90 million, going from Coinbase Institutional to regular Coinbase. While incoming coins could suggest selling intentions, many internal transfers are routine custody actions. A reversal in ETH’s price trend is likely the first step in getting buyers back on board. Historically, ETF flows have closely followed price movements. Despite recent struggles, ETH is still up 21.6% over the last 90 days, so a price recovery could reignite momentum and interest among investors. More ETFs offering staking may also encourage yield-seeking holders to switch funds while keeping their investments in ETH. Additionally, progress on the Glamsterdam upgrade could inspire renewed confidence if a new date is announced. Notably, weekly outflows have fallen sharply from $542.1 million to $320 million, then to $225 million, suggesting buyers may be poised to return. Should this trend turn into a week of net inflows while ETH stabilizes, Coinbase’s forthcoming quarterly report should reveal the true impact of the ETF selling trend. A few specific catalysts could flip the trend, but investors are watching closely for the first sign. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. Investors have pulled about $1.1 billion from U.S. spot Ether ( CRYPTO: ETH ) ETFs over the last three weeks, and the selling hasn’t stopped . These funds directly hold ETH, so when investors withdraw, they often have to sell coins to meet demand. This situation has also significantly impacted Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ), which serves as the custodian for most U.S. spot crypto ETFs. On October 23, 2026, Coinbase shares closed at about $164, down 17% over the past month. So what could attract ETF buyers back into the market? Ethereum spot ETFs have steadily lost funds, with net outflows of $542.1 million recorded from October 5 to 9, according to SoSoValue. Another $320 million followed in outflows from October 12 to 16. The trend persisted with an additional $225 million leaving over just four trading days from October 19 to 22, including a striking $110.5 million on October 22 alone. The complete figures for October 23 are still pending. Notably, one fund drove most of the withdrawals. BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ: ETHA ) saw approximately $1.01 billion exit during this timeframe, accounting for about 93% of the total outflows. Its net assets fell from roughly $9.9 billion on October 5 to around $7.8 billion on October 23—the day it recorded zero flows. Between October 19 and October 22, ETHA’s withdrawals totaled about $233 million, surpassing the $225 million total outflow for all funds in the same period. This suggests that while money is moving out of ETHA, some investors are reallocating their funds to other Ether ETFs, keeping their investment within the Ethereum ecosystem. Yield competition is the first factor. Many investors are attracted to staking options , which involve locking up ETH to help secure the Ethereum network in exchange for rewards. Staking funds distribute this yield to their shareholders. BlackRock also manages the iShares Staked Ethereum Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: ETHB ), meaning traditional Ether funds now compete with income-focused options. Falling prices are the second. ETH has dropped 11.5% in October, trading around $2,361 and is down 20% year-to-date. Falling prices can trigger ETF redemptions, creating a cycle of further selling pressure. Development delays are the third. On October 22, Ethereum developers announced a delay in the Glamsterdam upgrade’s test on the Hoodi network, initially scheduled for October 26. The Ethereum Foundation said developers need more time to assess how a proposed change interacts with existing smart contracts. Without a new timeline, this is another setback for ETH holders seeking immediate catalysts. Despite these outflows, the funds still hold $14.6 billion in net assets, compared to $12.7 billion in total net inflows. This discrepancy exists because ETH prices have risen since most of that investment was made, meaning early holders may still see profits despite recent downturns. Coinbase benefits from custody and ETH staking, so a decline in ETH demand affects its revenue streams. In its Q2 2026 earnings report released on July 30, Coinbase reported an 18.5% year-over-year revenue drop to $1.22 billion. Platform assets also fell from $294 billion to $246 billion, with executives citing ETF outflows as a contributing factor. In discussions with analysts, Coinbase’s Alesia Haas stated, “When customers store with us, they transact with us.” This works both ways—fewer stored assets reduce trading revenue. Over the past week, Coinbase’s stock slipped 5%, while it’s down 27.3% year-to-date. Large transactions have also drawn attention. Whale Alert reported transfers such as 38,236 ETH, valued at $91.7 million, moving into Coinbase Institutional and another 37,568 ETH, worth $90 million, going from Coinbase Institutional to regular Coinbase. While incoming coins could suggest selling intentions, many internal transfers are routine custody actions. A reversal in ETH’s price trend is likely the first step in getting buyers back on board. Historically, ETF flows have closely followed price movements. Despite recent struggles, ETH is still up 21.6% over the last 90 days, so a price recovery could reignite momentum and interest among investors. More ETFs offering staking may also encourage yield-seeking holders to switch funds while keeping their investments in ETH. Additionally, progress on the Glamsterdam upgrade could inspire renewed confidence if a new date is announced. Notably, weekly outflows have fallen sharply from $542.1 million to $320 million, then to $225 million, suggesting buyers may be poised to return. Should this trend turn into a week of net inflows while ETH stabilizes, Coinbase’s forthcoming quarterly report should reveal the true impact of the ETF selling trend. State Department this week issued a security alert that cautioned "Americans in Paris for the NFL game" to "exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings" because of protests.Leading up to the game, Steelers fans have been weighing whether to travel to Paris. One fan decided to change his trip to Madrid and Barcelona, saying for the amount of money he was spending, going to France would be "a roll of the dice." Meanwhile, two Steelers fans in Paris told KDKA that they're remaining cautious and haven't felt unsafe yet. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said this week that preparations were made in consultation with U.S. and French authorities. Street protests, he said, "are not unusual in France."On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron met with Goodell along with Saints owner Gayle Benson and Steelers owners Art Rooney II at the Élysée Palace to "discuss Sunday's game and the long-term future of the NFL in Paris."The NFL said Friday that its pop-up shop in the city center would be closed Saturday but that fans could use an alternative shop set up at Stade de France, located north of the city in Saint-Denis.The Steelers arrived in Paris on Friday while the Saints have been there since Monday.

The Pittsburgh Steelers , however, will depart following their practice on Thursday. But before their Week 7 matchup at Stade de France, Pittsburgh was supposed to host a house fan event in Paris. That event has now been cancelled, considering the ongoing riots in the country. “Following recent events in the Bastille neighborhood, and after careful consideration, we felt it appropriate not to move forward with the planned Steelers House fan event in Paris,” the statement read, per Jimmy English . “Preparations for Sunday’s NFL Paris game at Stade de France continue as planned, with NFL working closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters.” The decision came after The Associated Press reported on October 18 that approximately thousands of people took part in a protest march in the Paris region, while authorities estimated roughly 550,000 participants nationwide. Meanwhile, police said 855 people had been arrested in the Paris region after violent clashes and looting. Saints matchup became a topic of discussion due to safety concerns. The team’s decision to cancel its fan event, however, came because of the Bastille area. Per reports, the Bastille area was identified as the location of the Steelers House and a planned Saturday march. Meanwhile, the league clarified that the Paris game will go ahead despite the ongoing protest in France. “Preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France next Sunday. We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. There’s been no disruption or impact at league sites.” As the league’s statement came to light, the Saints supported the decision to move ahead with the game. The team’s vice president of communications, Greg Bensel, acknowledged that “We concur with the NFL’s statement and are planning to play the game.” Meanwhile, at the league’s fall meeting, NFL executive vice president Peter O’Reilly said the league was working with Parisian and national authorities, the U.S. He emphasized that the safety of teams, fans, and everyone involved was the league’s highest priority. O’Reilly also said league security officials, including senior vice president Cathy Lanier, were on the ground in France. Then, on Wednesday, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell told reporters that he had a high level of confidence in the safety arrangements for the game. “We’ve made all the preparations,” said Goodell, per AP News. “Protests are not unusual in France, as you know, and that’s something that we will be aware of and make sure that the appropriate arrangements are made.” The league has previously canceled its planned international games and moved them back to the United States for multiple reasons. In 2020, the NFL announced that all five scheduled international games- four in London and one in Mexico City- would instead be played in the U.S. because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Before, the league also moved the November 19, 2018, matchup between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Los Angeles Rams from Estadio Azteca to the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum because the playing surface failed to meet league standards. Saints matchup at Stade de France is scheduled for October 25. While the safety concerns are evident, the league is currently planning to move ahead with France’s first NFL regular-season game.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it. Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture. Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it. It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send. As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device. Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much . Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how . Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart. Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong. In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users. On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews. First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send.

As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device.

Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much .

Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how .

Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong.
In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users.

On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews.
While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session.

First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents.

Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. To prevent this, we recommend using our security solutions , which block visits to malicious and suspicious websites. We also suggest storing your credentials in Kaspersky Password Manager — our password manager won’t let you auto-fill saved logins and passwords on a fake site.

Users of Kaspersky Standard , Kaspersky Plus , and Kaspersky Premium have access to our Private Browsing feature (on Windows and macOS ). It prevents third-party services from tracking your online activity and collecting real-time information about what you do on websites.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it. Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture. Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it. It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. Additionally, real-time chat monitoring enables supervisors to oversee chat interactions, ensuring quality and timeliness.” While that might sound helpful and harmless to some, having their unsent messages watched without their permission can trigger outright panic for others. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send. As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device. Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much . Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how . Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart. Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong. In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users. On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews. While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session. First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents. Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. extraction.body: U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday. A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group Saturday, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu. Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month. Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . passages: US President Donald Trump’s defeat has turned into a domestic challenge as public dissatisfaction grows over the US war waged against Iran and the issue could impact the political standing of the Republicans ahead of the congressional midterm elections.
The same Pew Research Center poll found 52 percent of Americans have little or no confidence that the Trump administration will achieve its goals in the confrontation with Iran.
47 percent of participants predict that U.S. military action against Iran will continue for more than another year, while 30 percent expect the situation to last between six months and a year.
Trump weighing renewed strikes on Iran amid domestic opposition and economic pressure Midterm politics tied to Iran war; polls show public dissatisfaction

The first question in a US Senate debate in Michigan between Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers was about the issue that appears to matter most to voters, the economy, and El-Sayed linked it to the US-Israel war on Iran.

El-Sayed said on Wednesday, “Right now, the cost of gas, the cost of groceries, it all really goes back to this war in Iran,” and he called for a War Powers Resolution rather than a senator who wants to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war.
Trump’s new gamble.. does it end the Iran war or blow up the region?

Trump’s approval rating fell to its lowest level since the start of his second term between August 28 and September 1, and it said his national approval rating had fallen to 35% with 59% disapproval by August 31.
Trump claimed that 75,000 protesters had been killed in Iran by the regime over seven months and described the regime as “truly evil.”

President Trump is seeking, as the midterm elections on November 3 approach, to find justification for continuing military operations and the state of alert in the absence of a decisive settlement on the Iran war.
Trump claimed that 75,000 protesters had been killed in Iran by the regime over seven months and described the regime as “truly evil.”

Trump quoted writing on his Truth Social page: “They keep killing the protesters and everyone who stands in their way. I can only hope that the American people and the world at large realize how evil they are! Seventy‑five thousand protesters have been killed in less than seven months.”

Trump is studying a return to a military campaign against Iran through strikes that would last several days, in a gamble that sanctions and the blockade have driven the Iranian economy to the brink of collapse.

The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.

Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.

extraction.body: Wealthy bitcoin $BTC $84,459.46 holders are increasingly treating their cryptocurrency as an asset to borrow against and generate income from, marking a shift from speculation toward private banking, according to Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca. At the Gibraltar-based bank, customers are seeking cash without selling their bitcoin, putting some of their holdings into income-generating investments, or accumulating more $BTC through interest paid on dollar savings, he said. “Customers are looking for yield and alpha,” Rocca told CoinDesk in an interview, pointing to demand from funds and family offices for accumulation and income products. The behavior reflects bitcoin’s growing maturity, he said. Five or six years ago, the cryptocurrency was primarily viewed as a trading and speculative asset. Today, more holders want financial services built around their existing wealth. Xapo grew out of a bitcoin custody business known for its Swiss bunker storage. Its customers include early adopters who have experienced several halvings (the periodic reductions in new bitcoin issuance), and the rallies and downturns surrounding them. The bank charges an annual membership fee of $1,000, combining dollar banking with access to bitcoin custody, investments and borrowing. Experience has pushed those customers in different directions. Some of the earliest adopters became more willing to take profits as bitcoin reached record prices, having watched gains disappear in previous downturns, Rocca said. Others, including investors who entered around 2018 and 2019, remain determined to hold and prefer borrowing against their coins when they need liquidity. For the profit-takers, selling does not necessarily mean abandoning bitcoin. Some keep the proceeds in dollar savings accounts and receive interest in $BTC , gradually rebuilding their cryptocurrency holdings while retaining cash. Rocca said about 45% of Xapo customers use that feature. Xapo currently advertises a variable base rate of 4.1% on dollar savings, paid in bitcoin, alongside a temporary 4.6% introductory rate for eligible new members. It’s a separate bitcoin credit fund that targets annual returns of up to 4% through lending, exposing investors to credit and counterparty risk. The common thread is the demand to make existing wealth productive. “The theme of this cycle is yield, accumulation, income generation,” Rocca said. Borrowing allows customers to retain exposure to future bitcoin gains, although they also remain exposed to price declines while taking on debt. Traditional banks increasingly acknowledge that clients want bitcoin exposure, Rocca said. Their interest in custody and investment products represents a substantial change from the skepticism he encountered when he began working in crypto in 2016.

extraction.body: Wealthy bitcoin $BTC $84,459.46 holders are increasingly treating their cryptocurrency as an asset to borrow against and generate income from, marking a shift from speculation toward private banking, according to Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca. At the Gibraltar-based bank, customers are seeking cash without selling their bitcoin, putting some of their holdings into income-generating investments, or accumulating more $BTC through interest paid on dollar savings, he said. “Customers are looking for yield and alpha,” Rocca told CoinDesk in an interview, pointing to demand from funds and family offices for accumulation and income products. The behavior reflects bitcoin’s growing maturity, he said. Five or six years ago, the cryptocurrency was primarily viewed as a trading and speculative asset. Today, more holders want financial services built around their existing wealth. Xapo grew out of a bitcoin custody business known for its Swiss bunker storage. Its customers include early adopters who have experienced several halvings (the periodic reductions in new bitcoin issuance), and the rallies and downturns surrounding them. The bank charges an annual membership fee of $1,000, combining dollar banking with access to bitcoin custody, investments and borrowing. Experience has pushed those customers in different directions. Some of the earliest adopters became more willing to take profits as bitcoin reached record prices, having watched gains disappear in previous downturns, Rocca said. Others, including investors who entered around 2018 and 2019, remain determined to hold and prefer borrowing against their coins when they need liquidity. For the profit-takers, selling does not necessarily mean abandoning bitcoin. Some keep the proceeds in dollar savings accounts and receive interest in $BTC , gradually rebuilding their cryptocurrency holdings while retaining cash. Rocca said about 45% of Xapo customers use that feature. Xapo currently advertises a variable base rate of 4.1% on dollar savings, paid in bitcoin, alongside a temporary 4.6% introductory rate for eligible new members. It’s a separate bitcoin credit fund that targets annual returns of up to 4% through lending, exposing investors to credit and counterparty risk. The common thread is the demand to make existing wealth productive. “The theme of this cycle is yield, accumulation, income generation,” Rocca said. Borrowing allows customers to retain exposure to future bitcoin gains, although they also remain exposed to price declines while taking on debt. Traditional banks increasingly acknowledge that clients want bitcoin exposure, Rocca said. Their interest in custody and investment products represents a substantial change from the skepticism he encountered when he began working in crypto in 2016.

This exodus halted a three-day streak of inflows. Bitcoin's price also fell during this period. After closing at about $84,025 on October 21, it fell to $81,307 the next day and traded near $80,483 on the morning of October 24. The largest fund continued to see withdrawals in the following session, raising questions about whether the selling is over or just beginning. The iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ), managed by BlackRock, experienced the largest loss, with $254.1 million pulled out on October 22. Additionally, the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( CBOE: FBTC ) saw $217.5 million in withdrawals. Together, these two funds accounted for about 74% of that day's total outflows. Other smaller funds also experienced losses. The ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF ( CBOE: ARKB ) lost $109.4 million, the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust ( NYSEARCA: GBTC ) fell by $29.5 million, and the Bitwise Bitcoin ETF ( NYSEARCA:BITB ) lost $27.4 million. Notably, GBTC's relatively minor loss stands out; since it converted to an ETF in January 2024, the fund has seen about $28 billion more exit than enter, largely due to its higher fee of 1.5% compared to IBIT’s 0.25%. A net outflow indicates that investors cashed in more fund shares than they purchased. This typically forces the fund to sell or return Bitcoin to cover redemptions, increasing the supply of Bitcoin on the market. Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as the custodian for most of these funds, meaning it securely holds the coins. Traders closely watch its institutional wallets. Whale Alert, a service that tracks significant blockchain transfers, noted that 1,909 BTC ($155.7 million) and 789 BTC ($64.3 million) moved into Coinbase Institutional, while 2,163 BTC ($176.3 million) moved out to a new wallet. Typically, Bitcoin entering an exchange's institutional desk may suggest potential selling, while coins moving to a new wallet imply long-term storage. The recent transfers indicate mixed activity, with inbound amounts totaling about 2,698 BTC, roughly 535 BTC more than withdrawals. Meanwhile, Coinbase’s stock has taken a hit. On October 23, it closed at $164.45, down 2.7% for the day and 17% over the last month. In its second-quarter earnings report, Coinbase said assets on its platform fell to $246 billion from $294 billion, partly due to ETF outflows. CEO Brian Armstrong noted in a call on July 30 that "Bitcoin tends to cycle," adding that "it will come back in a big way at times." On October 23, IBIT recorded another $110.3 million in net outflows, according to SoSoValue, while FBTC saw $31.8 million withdrawn. The complete tally for all funds for that day was not yet available at the time of writing. Nevertheless, the weekly totals seem more encouraging. For the week ending October 22, the funds posted a net inflow of $442.7 million, up from $228.6 million in net outflows the previous week. This rapid shift reflects how quickly investor sentiment can change, similar to the $6.3 billion inflow run seen in Q3 following previous dips. The funds now hold $104.7 billion in net assets and have accumulated $57.3 billion in total net inflows. Bitcoin’s price chart sheds light on some of the current anxieties. While Bitcoin is down 4.4% over the past month and 7.8% year-to-date in 2026, it is still up by 23.4% over the last 90 days. Thus, some of the ETF selling may stem from profit-taking after this recent rally. However, Bitcoin remains approximately 36% below its all-time high of $126,080. Based on IBIT’s continued $110.3 million outflow on October 23, the selling doesn’t appear to be over yet. Despite IBIT's substantial net assets of around $65.8 billion, a string of negative days could add stress to the market. Notably, GBTC's relatively minor loss stands out; since it converted to an ETF in January 2024, the fund has seen about $28 billion more exit than enter, largely due to its higher fee of 1.5% compared to IBIT’s 0.25%.

A net outflow indicates that investors cashed in more fund shares than they purchased. This typically forces the fund to sell or return Bitcoin to cover redemptions, increasing the supply of Bitcoin on the market.

Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as the custodian for most of these funds, meaning it securely holds the coins. Traders closely watch its institutional wallets. Whale Alert, a service that tracks significant blockchain transfers, noted that 1,909 BTC ($155.7 million) and 789 BTC ($64.3 million) moved into Coinbase Institutional, while 2,163 BTC ($176.3 million) moved out to a new wallet.

CEO Brian Armstrong noted in a call on July 30 that "Bitcoin tends to cycle," adding that "it will come back in a big way at times."

On October 23, IBIT recorded another $110.3 million in net outflows, according to SoSoValue, while FBTC saw $31.8 million withdrawn. The complete tally for all funds for that day was not yet available at the time of writing.
Nevertheless, the weekly totals seem more encouraging. For the week ending October 22, the funds posted a net inflow of $442.7 million, up from $228.6 million in net outflows the previous week.

This rapid shift reflects how quickly investor sentiment can change, similar to the $6.3 billion inflow run seen in Q3 following previous dips. The funds now hold $104.7 billion in net assets and have accumulated $57.3 billion in total net inflows.

Bitcoin’s price chart sheds light on some of the current anxieties. While Bitcoin is down 4.4% over the past month and 7.8% year-to-date in 2026, it is still up by 23.4% over the last 90 days. passages: 7, Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) co-founder Joseph Lubin said on CNBC that while AI might offer creativity and expertise, it can't create trust, which blockchains like his can help to supply.
In his view, AI and crypto will thus end up merging, becoming the system where programmatic work can be commissioned, completed, and compensated.
The most likely scenario is that Ethereum's capital pulls agents in gradually, with payments flowing through its Layer-2 networks.
There's a little bit of evidence that Lubin's world is already starting to peek into existence.
Here's what it'd mean for Ethereum if that continues.
Today, one of Ethereum's biggest contributions to the AI-in-crypto segment is ERC-8004, a new standard for blockchains that calls for tracking the identities and reputations of AI agents.
